#10706. Testing JSON-LD Like an API: 7 Checks Before Your Next Release

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A content editor changes an article’s headline. The page updates immediately, but its JSON-LD still contains the previous title. A redesign introduces a new author component while an old plugin continues publishing a different author name in the page source.

Neither failure necessarily produces a JavaScript error. Both leave machines and readers with conflicting descriptions of the same page.

For developers, the useful approach is to treat JSON-LD as a maintained output of the application, with a data source, validation rules, and regression tests. This guide uses a blog template to show how. You will need basic JavaScript knowledge and a modern Node.js installation for the runnable tests.

Requests for search improvements often arrive as broad outcomes: improve discoverability, clarify entities, or support answer engines. These need to become implementation requirements before development starts.

For example, AEO directory includes structured data within descriptions of broader optimization services. For an engineering team, the actionable deliverable is a page representation whose types, properties, and values can be checked against the published content. I personally used this , and adding this because this can help other developer's and designer for optimization and get higher search result's.

For a blog template, define these acceptance criteria:

Keep implementation success separate from search outcomes. Google’s AI features guidance says there is no special Schema.org markup required for its AI search features. Correct markup also does not guarantee rich results or inclusion in an AI-generated answer.

Avoid separate, manually maintained copies of the headline, author, and publication date. Both the visible template and metadata builder should consume the same published record.

Save the following as article-schema.mjs. The builder assumes an upstream content-validation step has already checked required strings, timestamps, and approved HTTPS URLs.

This is a deliberately small example, not a complete rich-result eligibility checklist. Add relevant images and other supported properties when the real page supplies them. Consult the Schema.org BlogPosting definition and Google’s Article documentation for their respective vocabularies and search guidance.

Use a consistent canonical-URL policy before building the identifier: normalize the intended hostname, trailing-slash convention, and query parameters. Do not generate a fresh UUID for the same article on every request.

SitePoint’s guide to implementing JSON-LD on modern websites covers embedding approaches across common stacks.

Valid JSON is not automatically safe to insert into a raw HTML script element.

A CMS value containing can terminate the element at the HTML-parser level, even when the value belongs to a JSON string. Concatenating a headline directly into a script tag is particularly risky.

Append this helper to article-schema.mjs:

JSON serialization handles quotes and backslashes. Replacing literal less-than characters prevents an embedded closing-script sequence from appearing in the resulting text. The Next.js JSON-LD guide documents this approach for script embedding.

Use the serialized result as the content of a script element with type="application/ld+json". Follow your framework’s documented embedding mechanism so the JSON is neither double-encoded nor inserted through an unrelated HTML context.

This helper is specific to JSON-LD script content. It is not a general-purpose HTML sanitizer, URL validator, or substitute for validating CMS data.

The tests should catch changes that would make metadata misleading or unsafe, not merely confirm that an object exists.

Save this file as article-schema.test.mjs beside the builder:

These are unit tests for the builder and serializer. They do not prove that a template embeds the script correctly or that the deployed page is eligible for a search feature. SitePoint’s explanation of unit, functional, and integration testing helps distinguish those responsibilities.

A passing builder test cannot detect a page component reading a different CMS field.

Add a browser-level check against a controlled article fixture. Inspect its visible heading, byline, dates, canonical link, and JSON-LD together. For this template, assert that the intended article entity appears once and matches those visible fields.

Do not assert that the entire page contains exactly one JSON-LD script. A site may legitimately publish organization, breadcrumb, and article entities separately. Instead, identify the relevant entity by its @id and detect conflicting definitions.

Include these failure cases in the test plan:

Prefer generating metadata from the content loaded during server rendering or static generation when that fits the application. If it is injected client-side, inspect the rendered result and test navigation explicitly. Avoid making essential metadata depend on a user interaction.

No single tool establishes syntax, semantic accuracy, search eligibility, and content consistency at once.

Test both representative code samples and deployed URLs. A validator cannot confirm the truth of an author name simply because the property is syntactically valid.

Google’s general structured-data guidelines also require markup to represent the page accurately. Treat validation warnings as findings to investigate; do not add invented reviews, dates, or attributes merely to improve a tool’s output.

Ownership matters after the first release. Decide which application layer generates article markup, who maintains its mapping, and which publishing events invalidate cached output.

When an editor changes a headline, the visible page and JSON-LD should be rebuilt or refreshed together. Updating one while serving the other from an older cache creates a mismatch even if both implementations are individually correct.

Avoid setting dateModified to the current time on every deployment. A CSS update or infrastructure rebuild does not necessarily mean the article changed. Read the timestamp from the editorial record instead.

Before shipping a template change, run the builder tests, inspect one rendered page per affected template, and check representative deployed URLs. Keep a small fixture set that includes optional fields, long text, translated content, and script-like strings.

A reliable JSON-LD implementation has a traceable relationship with published content. When someone changes the page, its machine-readable description should change predictably—and the test suite should expose the cases where it does not.

#10703. How to Create an App in ChatGPT in 2026

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Learning how to create an app in ChatGPT starts with the Jotform App Builder plugin (listed in ChatGPT's plugin directory as Jotform Apps): install it, connect a Jotform account, describe the app, approve the requested action, and refine the result. The plugin creates a Jotform App containing pages, forms, and resources that can be edited in Jotform App Builder and shared with its intended audience.

ChatGPT helps turn an idea into a clear request and supports revisions through conversation. The Jotform App Builder plugin performs the app-building actions, while the App Builder in Jotform provides the editor for closer customization.

This no-code ChatGPT app builder workflow suits projects built around information, forms, and everyday tasks.

"ChatGPT app development" can also describe coding projects. OpenAI's documentation on building plugins for ChatGPT describes a package of skills, an optional MCP server that connects to tools and data through the Model Context Protocol, optional UI, authentication, and publishing. The two routes differ like this:

This article covers the no-code route. The result is a Jotform App; the workflow does not include writing and deploying a separate codebase.

A Jotform App can organize pages, forms, and resources for customers, employees, members, or event attendees. The most useful first project has one audience and one clear purpose. Here are some examples:

These are starting structures. A booking form, for example, still needs its availability settings checked. An ordering app needs its order process reviewed, and any payment setup requires separate attention.

Setup starts with installing the plugin in ChatGPT and authorizing access to the intended Jotform account. Jotform's own how-to guide lists the steps.

To create an app in ChatGPT, select the installed plugin in a new chat and enter a specific description. Include the audience, purpose, pages, and design direction.

This gives the AI app builder a defined structure. The studio should then supply its real booking URL, approved resource links, contact details, and onboarding copy during review. It is important to review every generated form, link, and business rule before use.

A good prompt explains who will use the app, what they need to accomplish, and which elements support that task. Visual preferences help, but purpose and content should come first.

"Build an app for my business" leaves the audience, structure, and actions unclear. The design-studio example identifies a client audience, an onboarding task, specific pages, and a color scheme. Before submitting a request, define:

Request the essentials to build a Jotform App around one process, then expand.

The plugin supports follow-up requests in the same chat. Smaller changes make it easier to review each update and identify anything that needs correction. For the studio onboarding app, some follow-ups could include:

Each request should be followed by a review of the result. A map needs the correct address; a gallery needs suitable images; a booking form needs appropriate fields and configuration.

Select Edit in Jotform when you need closer editing. In Jotform App Builder, inspect every page, element, form, link, label, and visual choice. Replace the sample content and check that navigation follows the client's expected path. Third-party integrations require manual setup in the builder, so requesting a booking feature should not be treated as confirmation that an external calendar has been connected.

Select Share App in the generated result to open the available sharing options. For detailed distribution and access settings, open the app in Jotform App Builder and use the Publish tab and Quick Share. Jotform's sharing guide covers each option.

The builder supports copying the app link, inviting people by email, social sharing, and downloading a QR code. Choose the method that fits your audience: a client can receive a link, while event attendees may find a QR code more useful.

Review access before distributing the app, because newly created apps are public by default. Check exactly what a visitor can open before publishing.

Test the Jotform App as an intended user would, using fictional information first. Review it on both desktop and mobile before collecting real submissions.

Creating an app with the plugin is free to start, and Jotform offers a free Starter plan, but app usage remains subject to your account's allowances. A Jotform support reply from 2024 describes Starter as up to five forms and 100 monthly submissions. These are account allowances, rather than a separate allocation for each generated app, and they may have changed, so confirm them on Jotform's current pricing page. Paid plans provide more submissions.

Before you launch, compare expected usage with the current account limits. An onboarding app serving a few clients has different requirements from an event app collecting hundreds of registrations.

The most common mistakes are unclear requests, oversized first versions, and sharing before testing. Each can be reduced by defining a smaller task and reviewing the result.

This workflow is best for defined business tasks. Projects requiring extensive custom backend behavior need a separate assessment, such as the developer route described above.

Before sharing, confirm that the app serves its intended audience and that its content, behavior, and settings have been reviewed. A short launch checklist helps keep the review consistent.

Here are some frequently asked questions about the output, account requirements, and practical limits of the Jotform App Builder plugin.

Yes. With the plugin installed and authorized, plain-language requests can generate and revise an app in ChatGPT.

The plugin can create a Jotform App combining pages, forms, and resources. Follow-up prompts can refine its structure, content, and design.

Customer portals, internal tools, event apps, business websites, directories, onboarding hubs, and booking or ordering apps are some of the suitable starting points.

Yes. Setup requires signing in to Jotform and authorizing the connection.

Yes. Further prompts support revisions in the same chat. Edit in Jotform opens the editor, and Share App provides sharing options.

Yes. The workflow supports forms and requests for booking forms, maps, FAQs, and galleries. Check their content and configuration before use.

A Jotform App is the finished app created and maintained through Jotform. A custom GPT configures a conversational assistant, while a plugin or application made with OpenAI developer tools involves a separate development workflow with its own build, authentication, and publishing steps.

Understanding how to create an app in ChatGPT means keeping the roles clear: ChatGPT supports the conversation, the plugin creates and revises the Jotform App, and the Jotform editor handles closer editing and configuration.

Start with a focused task, then review the content, permissions, and behavior. Test the complete experience with sample information before sharing it with the intended audience.

#10702. PaliGemma 2 Mix - New Instruction Vision Language Models by Google

Last December, Google released PaliGemma 2: a new family of pre-trained (pt) PaliGemma vision language models (VLMs) based on SigLIP and Gemma 2. The models come in three different sizes (3B, 10B, 28B) and three different resolutions (224x224, 448x448, 896x896).

Today, Google is releasing PaliGemma 2 mix: fine-tuned on a mix of vision language tasks, including OCR, long and short captioning and more.

PaliGemma 2 pretrained (pt) variants are great vision language models to transfer on a given task at hand. All pt checkpoints are meant to be fine-tuned on a downstream task and were released for that purpose.

The mix models give a quick idea of the performance one would get when fine-tuning the pre-trained checkpoints on a downstream task. The main purpose of the PaliGemma model family is to provide pretrained models that can learn better on a downstream task, instead of providing a versatile chat model. Mix models give a good signal of how pt models perform when fine-tuned on a mix of academic datasets.

You can read more about PaliGemma 2 in this blog post.

You can find all the mix models and the demo in this collection.

PaliGemma 2 mix models can accomplish a variety of tasks. We can categorize them according to their subtasks as follows.

Note that this list of subtasks is non-exhaustive, and you can get more information on the full list of tasks in the PaliGemma 2 paper.

When prompting PaliGemma 2 mix models, we can use open-ended prompts. In the previous iteration of PaliGemma pretrained models, we needed to add a task prefix to the prompt depending on the task we’d like to accomplish in a given language. This still works, but open-ended prompts yield better performance. Prompts with task prefix look like the following:

Only two tasks that work solely with task prefixes are object detection and image segmentation. The prompts look like the following.

If you want to immediately get started, feel free to jump to this section of the blog, or try the demo.

In this section, we will review the aforementioned capabilities, how PaliGemma 2 mix performs on them, and compare different variants with different sizes and resolutions on a few of the tasks. Here, we are testing the model on a few in-the-wild examples.

We have evaluated PaliGemma 2 mix variants according to their localization-related capabilities. Given a prompt “detect {object description};{another object description}” with different objects of interest, PaliGemma can detect different objects of interest. The prompt here is not limited to short classes like “bird,” but it can be “bird on a stick”.

Below, you can find detection and segmentation outputs of different variants with a fixed resolution of 448x448. We zoom in on the object of interest for visualization purposes.

You can use PaliGemma 2 mix models using transformers.

We have an in-depth tutorial on fine tuning PaliGemma 2. The same notebook can be used to fine tune the mix checkpoints as well.

We are releasing a demo for a 10B model with 448x448 resolution. You can play with it below or head to app in this link.

Read and learn more about PaliGemma models below.

We would like to thank Sayak Paul and Vaibhav Srivastav for the review of this blog post. We thank the Google team for releasing this amazing, and open, model family.

#10701. SmolVLM2: Bringing Video Understanding to Every Device

SmolVLM2 represents a fundamental shift in how we think about video understanding - moving from massive models that require substantial computing resources to efficient models that can run anywhere. Our goal is simple: make video understanding accessible across all devices and use cases, from phones to servers.

We are releasing models in three sizes (2.2B, 500M and 256M), MLX ready (Python and Swift APIs) from day zero. We've made all models and demos available in this collection.

Want to try SmolVLM2 right away? Check out our interactive chat interface where you can test visual and video understanding capabilities of SmolVLM2 2.2B through a simple, intuitive interface.

We are introducing three new models with 256M, 500M and 2.2B parameters. The 2.2B model is the go-to choice for vision and video tasks, while the 500M and 256M models represent the smallest video language models ever released.

While they're small in size, they outperform any existing models per memory consumption. Looking at Video-MME (the go-to scientific benchmark in video), SmolVLM2 joins frontier model families on the 2B range and we lead the pack in the even smaller space.

Video-MME stands out as a comprehensive benchmark due to its extensive coverage across diverse video types, varying durations (11 seconds to 1 hour), multiple data modalities (including subtitles and audio), and high-quality expert annotations spanning 900 videos totaling 254 hours. Learn more here.

Compared with the previous SmolVLM family, our new 2.2B model got better at solving math problems with images, reading text in photos, understanding complex diagrams, and tackling scientific visual questions. This shows in the model performance across different benchmarks:

When it comes to video tasks, 2.2B is a good bang for the buck. Across the various scientific benchmarks we evaluated it on, we want to highlight its performance on Video-MME where it outperforms all existing 2B models.

We were able to achieve a good balance on video/image performance thanks to the data mixture learnings published in Apollo: An Exploration of Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models

It’s so memory efficient, that you can run it even in a free Google Colab.

Nobody dared to release such small video models until today.

Our new SmolVLM2-500M-Video-Instruct model has video capabilities very close to SmolVLM 2.2B, but at a fraction of the size: we're getting the same video understanding capabilities with less than a quarter of the parameters 🤯.

And then there's our little experiment, the SmolVLM2-256M-Video-Instruct. Think of it as our "what if" project - what if we could push the boundaries of small models even further? Taking inspiration from what IBM achieved with our base SmolVLM-256M-Instruct a few weeks ago, we wanted to see how far we could go with video understanding. While it's more of an experimental release, we're hoping it'll inspire some creative applications and specialized fine-tuning projects.

To demonstrate our vision in small video models, we've built three practical applications that showcase the versatility of these models.

We make SmolVLM2 available to use with transformers and MLX from day zero. In this section, you can find different inference alternatives and tutorials for video and multiple images.

The easiest way to run inference with the SmolVLM2 models is through the conversational API – applying the chat template takes care of preparing all inputs automatically.

You can pass videos through a chat template by passing in {"type": "video", "path": {video_path}. See below for a complete example.

In addition to video, SmolVLM2 supports multi-image conversations. You can use the same API through the chat template, providing each image using a filesystem path, an URL, or a PIL.Image object:

To run SmolVLM2 with MLX on Apple Silicon devices using Python, you can use the excellent mlx-vlm library. First, you need to install mlx-vlm from this branch using the following command:

Then you can run inference on a single image using the following one-liner, which uses the unquantized 500M version of SmolVLM2:

We also created a simple script for video understanding. You can use it as follows:

Note that the system prompt is important to bend the model to the desired behaviour. You can use it to, for example, describe all scenes and transitions, or to provide a one-sentence summary of what's going on.

The Swift language is also supported through the mlx-swift-examples repo, which is what we used to build our iPhone app.

Until our in-progress PR is finalized and merged, you have to compile the project from this fork, and then you can use the llm-tool CLI on your Mac as follows.

Video analysis is also supported, as well as providing a system prompt. We found system prompts to be particularly helpful for video understanding, to drive the model to the desired level of detail we are interested in. This is a video inference example:

If you integrate SmolVLM2 in your apps using MLX and Swift, we'd love to know about it! Please, feel free to drop us a note in the comments section below!

You can fine-tune SmolVLM2 on videos using transformers 🤗 We have fine-tuned the 500M variant in Colab on video-caption pairs in VideoFeedback dataset for demonstration purposes. Since the 500M variant is small, it's better to apply full fine-tuning instead of QLoRA or LoRA, meanwhile you can try to apply QLoRA on cB variant. You can find the fine-tuning notebook here.

We would like to thank Raushan Turganbay, Arthur Zucker and Pablo Montalvo Leroux for their contribution of the model to transformers.

We are looking forward to seeing all the things you'll build with SmolVLM2! If you'd like to learn more about the SmolVLM family of models, feel free to read the following:

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Learning to code can feel overwhelming at first. There are different programming languages, development tools, and concepts to understand, and choosing where to begin is not always easy. Coding apps can make the process more approachable by breaking lessons into smaller steps and giving beginners a place to practice what they learn.

Whether you want to build websites, develop software, or explore programming as a new skill, the right app can help you get started. Some platforms focus on interactive lessons, while others offer coding exercises, guided projects, or access to a full development environment.

Here are six coding apps worth considering if you're learning programming for the first time.

Mimo is a beginner-friendly coding app designed to help users learn programming through short lessons and interactive exercises. Rather than starting with lengthy explanations, it introduces concepts in manageable steps, making it easier to fit learning into a busy schedule.

The app covers several topics, including Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and SQL. This makes it useful for beginners who want to explore general programming or focus on web development. As learners progress, they can work through structured learning paths and practice applying concepts through coding exercises and projects.

Mimo is particularly suitable for people who prefer a guided learning experience instead of figuring out what to study next on their own. Its mobile-first approach also makes it convenient to practice during breaks or while traveling.

A free starting option is available, although access to some courses and features requires a paid plan.

Best for: Beginners who want structured lessons and practical coding exercises.

SoloLearn is a coding education platform that helps beginners explore programming languages through short lessons, quizzes, and hands-on practice. It is a useful starting point for people who want to understand programming fundamentals before committing to a specific development path.

The platform offers courses in languages and technologies such as Python, JavaScript, Java, C++, SQL, HTML, and CSS. Its bite-sized lessons make complicated topics easier to approach, while interactive exercises let learners test their understanding as they progress.

Another useful feature is its learning community, where users can explore other people's code, participate in discussions, and learn from different approaches to programming problems.

SoloLearn works well for people who are still deciding which language to learn. However, completing lessons alone is not enough to develop strong programming skills. Beginners should also practice writing their own programs and building small projects.

The platform offers free learning options alongside paid features.

Best for: Beginners who want to explore multiple programming languages and learn through short, interactive lessons.

Codecademy Go is the mobile companion to Codecademy's online learning platform. It is designed to help learners reinforce programming concepts and review material while away from their computers.

Codecademy's broader learning platform offers courses covering web development, Python, JavaScript, SQL, and other technical subjects. The mobile app can be useful for reviewing concepts, practicing through supported activities, and maintaining a consistent learning routine between longer study sessions.

For example, someone taking a JavaScript course on a computer can use the mobile experience to revisit concepts and strengthen their understanding before returning to practical exercises.

It is important to distinguish between learning on a mobile device and developing software on one. Codecademy Go is primarily a companion for learning and review rather than a complete replacement for a desktop coding environment.

Some learning content is available without a subscription, while access to additional courses and features depends on the current plan.

Best for: Learners who want to review programming concepts alongside a structured online course.

Programming Hub is an educational app for people who want to explore programming and related technical subjects in one place. It brings together lessons, examples, and exercises designed to introduce users to different areas of software development.

Its learning material covers languages such as Python, Java, C++, and JavaScript, along with web development and other computing topics. This variety can be helpful for beginners who want to compare different languages before choosing one to study in depth.

The app's lesson-based approach makes it possible to explore a topic without immediately installing a development environment or configuring complicated software. Code examples and practice activities can also help learners connect theoretical concepts with practical applications.

However, beginners should avoid jumping between too many languages at once. Starting with one language, understanding its fundamentals, and applying those skills to a small project will generally provide a stronger foundation.

Programming Hub offers free and paid options, with access depending on the selected plan.

Best for: Beginners who want an introduction to several programming languages and computing topics.

Enki takes a slightly different approach to learning programming by emphasizing regular practice and the development of technical skills over time. Its lessons and exercises are designed to help users strengthen their understanding through consistent, manageable learning sessions.

Depending on the learning content available, users can explore topics such as Python, SQL, JavaScript, data analysis, and other areas of technology. This makes the app relevant to both aspiring developers and people who want to improve their technical knowledge for work.

One advantage of short, recurring practice sessions is that they encourage learners to revisit concepts instead of studying them once and moving on. Regular revision can help reinforce programming syntax, terminology, and problem-solving techniques.

Enki may be especially useful for people who already have some exposure to coding and want to maintain a learning habit. Complete beginners should check whether the available lessons match their chosen language and current skill level before starting.

The app offers different access options, so check its current listing for details about free and paid features.

Best for: Learners who prefer regular practice and gradual improvement in technical skills.

Replit is a browser-based development platform that allows users to write, run, and test code without setting up a traditional development environment on their computer. It is particularly useful for beginners who want to move beyond lessons and start creating their own programs.

Users can work with languages and technologies such as Python, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, depending on the project and environment. Instead of only answering quiz questions, learners can experiment with code, identify errors, and see how their changes affect a working application.

For example, a beginner learning Python could create a simple calculator, while someone studying web development could build a basic personal website. Starting with small projects helps learners understand how individual programming concepts work together.

Replit also provides AI-assisted development features, which can help users explore ideas and understand code. However, beginners should review generated code and learn why it works rather than relying on automated suggestions without understanding them.

Replit offers a free starting option, with additional capabilities available through paid plans. Features and usage limits may vary.

Best for: Beginners who want to practice writing code and experiment with real projects in a development environment.

The best coding app depends on your learning goals, preferred learning style, and current experience. Before choosing one, consider what you want to accomplish.

Choose a language first. If you want to learn general programming, Python is a reasonable starting point. If your goal is to build websites, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are more directly relevant.

Consider how you learn. Apps such as Mimo and SoloLearn emphasize short lessons and interactive practice. Codecademy Go is useful for reviewing course material, while Replit provides an environment for experimenting with code.

Look for practical exercises. Understanding a lesson is only the beginning. Choose resources that encourage you to write code, solve problems, and apply concepts in small projects.

Check the cost. Several coding apps provide free introductory content, but some courses and advanced features may require subscriptions. Review the current pricing before committing to a paid plan.

Move beyond the app. As your skills improve, practice using a computer, read technical documentation, and create projects of your own. These activities help you develop the problem-solving skills required for real programming work.

Coding apps provide an accessible way to begin learning programming without needing extensive technical knowledge or complicated software installations. They can help you understand basic concepts, practice regularly, and discover which areas of development interest you most.

Mimo and SoloLearn are worth exploring if you prefer guided lessons, while Codecademy Go can complement a structured course. Programming Hub and Enki offer alternative approaches to learning and practice, and Replit provides a way to experiment with working code.

You do not need to master every programming language or use several apps simultaneously. Start with one resource, focus on a single learning goal, and gradually apply what you learn to practical projects. Consistent practice and curiosity will take you further than simply completing lessons.

#10699. SigLIP 2: A better multilingual vision language encoder

Today Google releases a new and better family of multilingual vision-language encoders, SigLIP 2. The authors have extended the training objective of SigLIP (sigmoid loss) with additional objectives for improved semantic understanding, localization, and dense features.

SigLIP 2 models outperform the older SigLIP ones at all model scales in core capabilities, including zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, and transfer performance when extracting visual representations for Vision-Language Models (VLMs).

A cherry on top is the dynamic resolution (naflex) variant. This is useful for downstream tasks sensitive to aspect ratio and resolution.

Here is a list of all the models released:

Vision encoders are simple - they take an image, encode it into a representation, and that representation is used for downstream tasks like classification, object detection, image segmentation, and more vision tasks. Researchers are always in pursuit of visual representations that are dense, locality-aware, and semantically rich.

CLIP and ALIGN are the first examples of image encoders and text encoders aligned together through joint training. This approach opened new ways to train vision models. SigLIP took it further, replacing CLIP's contrastive loss with sigmoid loss for even better encoders.

The takeaway? With smarter training objectives, we keep building vision encoders that are more structured, fine-grained, and powerful. SigLIP 2 is just that, a bunch of really interesting and smart training objectives applied on top of that of SigLIP's to provide better and stronger vision language encoders.

We will try something new with this blog post. Rather than stating what is new and where to find it, we will go through a little exercise together. We start off with SigLIP and then brainstorm a series of questions (prefixed with 🤔) and answers (a new heading) to gradually cover all the updates in SigLIP 2. Sounds good?

We will begin our journey with the vision encoder where the patch size is 16, and the image resolution is 256. We have four variants to start our training:

🤔 Question 1: What is a (low effort) auxiliary training objective that we can use to learn better visual representations (in terms of location awareness and sense of locality)?

Let’s add a decoder to the mix. Now we have an image encoder, a text encoder, and a text decoder. The text decoder will have three objectives:

The decoder provides an additional signal to the vision encoder, making it location-aware. This marks the first improvement to the training recipe in SigLIP 2.

🤔 Question 2: How do we improve fine-grained local semantics of the image representation?

To improve fine-grained local semantics in image representation, we introduce two key training objectives, Global-Local Loss, and Masked Prediction Loss. Taking inspiration from self-supervised learning literature, we use self-distillation. We can use a model as a teacher, and the same model as a student. Upon each iteration the teacher will be the moving average of the student's parameters.

These objectives teach the vision encoder to be spatially aware and improve its local semantics. The authors add this loss only after 80% of the training is done with the sigmoid and decoder loss. This is done in order to save compute (additional losses are pretty expensive) and to not negatively affect the encoders.

🤔 Question 3: How to adapt models to different resolutions?

It is a known fact that image models can be very sensitive to varying resolutions and aspect ratios. Here we can leverage two distinct methodologies to adapt these models on different resolutions and patch sizes.

Models with the -naflex suffix are the dynamic resolution variants. While the fixed-resolution models can be used out of the box with the existing SiglipModel class, you would need to use Siglip2Model to use the naflex variants. We handle this automatically when you use the pipeline API!

This brings us to the end of the evolution from SigLIP to SigLIP 2. In the next sections we will look at applications with SigLIP 2.

Running inference on the models is pretty straightforward. You can copy paste the code below and run inference on a free tier Colab notebook 🚀

To run inference on SigLIP 2, please install transformers from main or from this stable branch: pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers@v4.49.0-SigLIP-2

Here we use the handy pipeline API to showcase zero-shot classification capabilities for SigLIP 2.

You can also encode images using the following:

Looking at the table of all the SigLIP 2 models released, we see two distinct changes from SigLIP:

The evaluation table of SigLIP 2 demonstrates its superiority over SigLIP.

Here is a demo where one can compare the zero-shot classification results of SigLIP 1 and SigLIP 2.

Vision encoders aligned to textual information have become increasingly vital in the development of Vision Language Models (VLMs). A common approach to building VLMs involves combining a pretrained vision encoder with a pretrained LLM, and training them together using multimodal data across a diverse set of vision-language tasks.

One standout example of a VLM leveraging the SigLIP family of vision encoders is PaliGemma. One can dive deeper into PaliGemma's capabilities in this PaliGemma blog post. Building on this foundation, the recently introduced PaliGemma 2 takes it a step further by integrating SigLIP with the advanced Gemma 2 LLM. It would be really exciting to swap out SigLIP with SigLIP 2 in a PaliGemma like setting and see how that model fares.

We would like to thank Michael Tschannen (first author of SigLIP 2), Vaibhav Srivastav and Sayak Paul for feedback on this blog post. A huge shout out to the Google team for releasing this amazing, and open, model family.

In no particular order we would like to thank Pavel, Ross, Pablo, Pedro, Lysandre and the rest of the Hugging Face team for their immense support and contribution towards this project.

#10698. Remote VAEs for decoding with Inference Endpoints 🤗

(This post was authored by hlky and Sayak)

When operating with latent-space diffusion models for high-resolution image and video synthesis, the VAE decoder can consume quite a bit more memory. This makes it hard for the users to run these models on consumer GPUs without going through latency sacrifices and others alike.

For example, with offloading, there is a device transfer overhead, causing delays in the overall inference latency. Tiling is another solution that lets us operate on so-called “tiles” of inputs. However, it can have a negative impact on the quality of the final image.

Therefore, we want to pilot an idea with the community — delegating the decoding process to a remote endpoint.

No data is stored or tracked, and code is open source. We made some changes to huggingface-inference-toolkit and use custom handlers.

This experimental feature is developed by Diffusers 🧨

Below, we cover three use cases where we think this remote VAE inference would be beneficial.

First, we have created a helper method for interacting with Remote VAEs.

Install diffusers from main to run the code. pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers@main

Here, we show how to use the remote VAE on random tensors.

Usage for Flux is slightly different. Flux latents are packed so we need to send the height and width.

But we want to use the VAE on an actual pipeline to get an actual image, not random noise. The example below shows how to do it with SD v1.5.

One of the great benefits of using a remote VAE is that we can queue multiple generation requests. While the current latent is being processed for decoding, we can already queue another one. This helps improve concurrency.

These tables demonstrate the VRAM requirements with different GPUs. Memory usage % determines whether users of a certain GPU will need to offload. Offload times vary with CPU, RAM and HDD/NVMe. Tiled decoding increases inference time.

If you like the idea and feature, please help us with your feedback on how we can make this better and whether you’d be interested in having this kind of feature more natively integrated into the Hugging Face ecosystem. If this pilot goes well, we plan on creating optimized VAE endpoints for more models, including the ones that can generate high-resolution videos!

#10697. AI, DevOps and the Cost of Hosting: From Idea to Production for $0

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An AI coding agent rebuilt my photo-collage app as a distributed system and deployed it to a free server. The hard part turned out to be hardware: one free ARM CPU, 538 collages created during load testing, zero failed jobs, and $0 a month.

Like most developers, I have never been short of product ideas. Hosting them has always been the problem. I have tried shared hosting with SmartWeb, Azure free credits, Google Compute Engine’s free VM instances, SmartWeb’s virtual private servers, and Heroku dynos. None of them left me satisfied. The worst experience was a $200 charge for an AI address API on Google Cloud—for an application that never earned me a single kobo.

I am not a cheapskate, but I learned quickly that one of the easiest ways to kill a potentially good idea is to get the finances wrong. An application has to stay online until it reaches a critical mass of users, and hosting an untested, unverified product on expensive hardware can be wasteful.

Agentic AI coding has changed how quickly I can move from idea to production. Over about five weeks of intermittent coding—amounting to roughly three days of full work with Claude—my photo-stitching app went from an Angular 8 project that would not even build to a distributed system running in production.

Along the way, Claude upgraded the front end from Angular 8 to Angular 22 and fixed the build on Node 24. It set up RabbitMQ with Docker Compose so the message broker configures itself on startup, and added real-time notifications over SignalR with a progress spinner. It fixed a crash loop caused by an unreadable iPhone photo. It redesigned the system so any server can process any job, with switchable database and file storage, direct browser-to-storage uploads, and photos resized in the browser before upload. It added reliability work that a team might debate for a sprint: a dead-letter queue, confirmed publishing, idempotent workers, recovery of stuck jobs, and automatic clean-up. It fixed the stitching so photos keep their proportions and borders are even. It wrote 41 automated tests and scrubbed leaked passwords and personal photos from the Git history.

Coding, QA, DevOps, and production support used to be separate phases, often handled by separate people. Here they happened in one conversation. When code becomes this cheap to produce, the bottleneck moves. For me, it moved to hardware.

To check what the AI builds, you have to run it locally. A distributed app means running the whole system locally: a web app, a background worker, a message broker, a database, and storage emulators. Because Claude adds features quickly, and each one can add another container, it is easy to exhaust a laptop’s RAM and CPU.

My setup made this lesson concrete. I work on a MacBook Air, with Visual Studio in a Windows virtual machine. Docker cannot run inside that VM on Apple Silicon, so Claude ran Docker on the Mac and drove it from Windows over SSH. Later, my mobile connection started dropping large packets and broke uploads from the VM, so Claude moved the load testing onto the server itself. The software problems took minutes. The hardware and network problems took longer.

Then comes hosting. Heroku looked like the easy route, but it has had no free dynos since 2022. The cheapest option is an Eco dyno at about $5 a month, plus about $5 for Postgres. That is affordable, but running it for an idea that has no users yet did not seem prudent.

Claude suggested Oracle Cloud’s Always Free tier: an ARM server with up to 4 CPUs and 24 GB of RAM, free with no end date. I created a small instance with 1 CPU and about 6 GB. Claude wrote a production Docker Compose file and a one-command setup script: Caddy as the gateway, the web app, the stitching worker, RabbitMQ, and PostgreSQL, with data that survives restarts. My repository is private, so rather than put a GitHub token on a public server, it copied the code over SSH and deployed it. The last blocker was mine to fix: opening ports 80 and 443 in Oracle’s network firewall. Then the site was live.

I did not want to guess, so I asked Claude to load-test the live server. Simulated users ran the full flow: upload two photos, wait for the real-time notification, and download the stitched collage.

The server handled 64 people creating collages at the same moment without a single failed job: 538 collages, zero errors. Its ceiling was about 62 collages a minute—one per second. Beyond that, users queue. With 4 people creating at once, 95% of collages arrived within about five seconds; at 64, each person waited about a minute. If each active user makes a collage every couple of minutes, one CPU comfortably serves around 85 people at once, and a few hundred if they use it less often.

The test also showed what runs out first, and it is not the CPU. Each collage stores about 5 MB, mostly the PNG output, so at full speed the disk would fill in under two hours. Switching to JPEG and shortening retention fixes that, and when traffic grows, three more free CPUs are waiting. That is the value of measuring before paying: I know what to change, and when.

Oracle isn’t being charitable. Servers need applications to run—ideally ones that go viral—and the free tier is a play for loyalty. Oracle wants successful projects to stay and grow into its paid services instead of moving off the platform once they reach critical mass. It can also reclaim free instances that sit idle.

I think the bet is smart, and it points to a bigger trend. AI-generated code still needs energy to run and hardware to host it, even when far fewer people work on each project. As more people turn ideas into working software, demand for compute will keep growing, and I expect hosting and data centres to become a very profitable business.

For now, the combination works: Claude orchestrates the coding, QA, and DevOps, and Oracle’s free server keeps an idea online long enough to find out whether it deserves to grow.

#10695. HuggingFace, IISc partner to supercharge model building on India's diverse languages

The Indian Institute of Science IISc and ARTPARK partner with Hugging Face to enable developers across the globe to access Vaani, India's most diverse open-source, multi-modal, multi-lingual dataset. Both organisations share a commitment to building inclusive, accessible, and state-of-the-art AI technologies that honor linguistic and cultural diversity.

The partnership between Hugging Face and IISc/ARTPARK aims to increase the accessibility and improve usability of the Vaani dataset, encouraging the development of AI systems that better understand India's diverse languages and cater to the digital needs of its people.

Launched in 2022 by IISc/ARTPARK and Google, Project Vaani is a pioneering initiative aimed at creating an open-source multi-modal dataset that truly represents India's linguistic diversity. This dataset is unique in its geo-centric approach, allowing for the collection of dialects and languages spoken in remote regions rather than focusing solely on mainstream languages.

Vaani targets the collection of over 150,000 hours of speech and 15,000 hours of transcribed text data from 1 million people across all 773 districts, ensuring diversity in language, dialects, and demographics.

The dataset is being built in phases, with Phase 1 covering 80 districts, which has already been open-sourced. Phase 2 is currently underway, expanding the dataset to 100 more districts, further strengthening Vaani's reach and impact across India's diverse linguistic landscape.

Key Highlights of the Vaani data set, open sourced so far: (as of 15-02-2025)

The Vaani dataset shows a rich distribution of languages across India's districts, highlighting linguistic diversity at a local level. This information is valuable for researchers, AI developers, and language technology innovators looking to build speech models tailored to specific regions and dialects. To explore the detailed district-wise language distribution, visit: Vaani Dataset on HuggingFace

If you need to access only transcribed data and you would like to skip untranscribed audio-only data, a subset of the larger dataset has been open sourced here. This dataset has 790 Hrs of transcribed audio, from ~7L speakers covering 70K images. This resource includes smaller, segmented audio units matched with precise transcriptions, allowing for different tasks including:

This additional dataset complements the main Vaani dataset, making it possible to develop end-to-end speech recognition systems and more targeted AI solutions.

The Vaani dataset offers several key advantages, including extensive language coverage (54 languages), representation across diverse geographical regions, diverse educational and socio economic background, very large speaker coverage, spontaneous speech data, and real-life data collection environments. These features can enable inclusive AI models for:

These AI models can power a wide range of Conversational AI applications. From educational tools to telemedicine platforms, healthcare solutions, voter helplines, media localization, and multilingual smart devices, the Vaani dataset can be a game-changer in real-world scenarios.

IISc/ARTPARK and Google have extended the partnership to Phase 2 (additional 100 districts). With this, Vaani covers all states in India! We are excited to bring this dataset to all of you.

The map highlights the districts across India where data has been collected as of Feb 5,2025

The most meaningful contribution you can make is to use the Vaani dataset. Whether building new AI applications, conducting research, or exploring innovative use cases, your engagement helps improve and expand the project.

We would be delighted to hear from you if you have feedback or insights from using the dataset. Please reach out to vaanicontact@gmail.com to share your experiences/inquire about collaboration opportunities or please do fill out this feedback form.

#10694. Building a Human Review Pipeline for AI Search: A Practical Developer’s Guide

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An AI search feature can return valid JSON, render correctly, and still give an unhelpful answer.

Imagine a documentation assistant answering a question about an API's current authentication requirements. It retrieves an outdated page, summarizes it fluently, and displays a citation. Every technical component appears to work, but the user receives instructions that no longer apply.

Automated checks are valuable, yet they cannot replace a clearly defined judgment about whether an answer solves the user's problem.

This guide builds a human-review workflow for a hypothetical API documentation assistant. You will define a review rubric, validate submissions with Python, measure reviewer disagreement, and turn accepted judgments into regression cases. The Python examples use Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn; they do not require a model-provider API key.

Start by identifying the failure you want to detect.

A documentation assistant usually has several stages: receive a question, retrieve relevant documents, generate an answer, and present that answer with supporting material.

Do not collapse these into a single “good answer” rating. A low score without a reason tells the team little about what to fix.

SitePoint’s introduction to retrieval-augmented generation provides background on how retrieval and generation fit together.

Preserve the exact question, answer revision, retrieved passages, document versions, and retrieval timestamp for each run. Store a snapshot manifest with stable passage IDs, source URLs, and content hashes. Reviewers should see the material supplied to that run, not today’s edited page. Keep the model and prompt configuration with the run so a later review can be traced to the behavior it evaluated.

A useful rubric defines observable criteria and separates evidence support from task completion and source suitability. Give each review the same user task and expected API version. Otherwise, reviewers may judge different questions while appearing to disagree about one answer.

For an answer about API authentication, use separate labels such as:

Supported: every material factual claim is backed by the supplied evidence.

Partially supported: some material claims lack support, while others are grounded.

Unsupported: the answer's central instruction lacks support or contradicts the evidence.

Cannot assess: the necessary evidence is missing, unreadable, or inaccessible.

Define task completion independently as complete, incomplete, or cannot assess. For source suitability, use suitable, outdated, or cannot assess. An answer can faithfully summarize an obsolete page while failing the request for current instructions.

Consider a fictional API migration: version 2 accepts X-API-Key, while version 3 requires Authorization: Bearer . If the supplied evidence contains only the version 2 page, an answer repeating X-API-Key can be supported by its evidence but still use an outdated source. If the evidence explicitly requires Bearer and the answer invents X-API-Key, label the answer unsupported. These are different engineering failures.

Also establish what reviewers should do when the source is outdated. They may correctly conclude that an answer reflects its evidence while separately flagging that evidence as unsuitable for the user's current task.

Start with a calibration batch covering clear successes, unsupported claims, missing evidence, and version mismatches. Have two reviewers label the same items independently, then compare their reasons. Revise ambiguous definitions before increasing volume; the batch is for improving the rubric, not estimating production quality.

Keep a rubric version on every review. Labels produced under different definitions should not be mixed without checking comparability.

A spreadsheet can help during exploration, but an engineering pipeline needs a stable record format.

Pydantic can validate a review record before it enters the dataset. Install Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn in your project environment, then use this model:

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError

model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True)

answer_revision: str = Field(min_length=1)

completion: Literal["complete", "incomplete", "cannot_assess"]

source_fit: Literal["suitable", "outdated", "cannot_assess"]

rationale: str = Field(min_length=20, max_length=2000)

Strict mode limits type coercion, and extra="forbid" rejects unexpected fields. The model checks shape and allowed values; it cannot establish that a judgment is correct. A minimum rationale length does not guarantee a useful explanation. The snapshot ID references a manifest, which can also record that retrieval produced no usable passages.

On the server, resolve the item, answer revision, snapshot, and passage IDs against the stored run. Reject IDs that do not belong together. Obtain the reviewer identity from the authenticated session rather than trusting a submitted reviewer_id. Store a server-generated submission time and preserve review revisions instead of silently overwriting earlier judgments.

Run this after the model definition. It accepts one fictional review and rejects both an unknown label and an extra field:

"rationale": "The answer invents X-API-Key; p1 requires Bearer.",

raise AssertionError("Invalid review was accepted")

The expected error types are literal_error and extra_forbidden. Add separate integration tests for mismatched evidence IDs, unauthorized submissions, and retries. Use a database uniqueness rule or an idempotency key so a repeated request does not create a second independent review.

More reviews do not automatically produce better evidence. If a task is ambiguous, scaling it can simply reproduce the ambiguity.

The workflow needs clear eligibility requirements, examples, escalation routes, and acceptance criteria. Reviewers assessing API behavior may need domain knowledge that general writing fluency does not provide.

If you work with an external AI-data contributor service such as Acquirox, define the task contract before assigning work: required expertise, permitted source material, output fields, and escalation rules. Keep ownership of the rubric, evaluation set, and acceptance decisions within the product team. Contributor capacity alone does not establish expertise in the API being reviewed.

Pilot the actual task in the review interface. Track drafts, submitted reviews, items needing adjudication, and final decisions as distinct workflow states. Reviewer judgments should remain immutable once submitted; corrections should create a new revision with a reason. Keep adjudication separate from the original labels.

For data involving users or contributors, document permitted uses, access boundaries, and retention. Remove credentials and unnecessary personal information from review material. An internal support transcript should not become a broadly accessible annotation task by accident.

Distinguish annotation from usability research. A skilled reviewer can judge whether an answer is supported, but that does not prove a first-time user can understand the interface.

SitePoint’s guide to choosing usability tests and participants offers related guidance on matching participants and methods to the question being investigated.

The review interface shapes the data it collects.

Label Studio is an option for configurable labeling interfaces and data import/export. If you use it, map exported annotations into the Review schema through an adapter; do not assume its export structure matches your application contract. A custom interface may be appropriate when reviewers need API-version navigation or passage-level citations.

The original question and relevant user context.

The evidence snapshot supplied to the model.

Separate controls for support and task completion.

A rationale field and an explicit “cannot assess” option.

Display stable passage IDs beside the evidence and let reviewers attach those IDs to their rationale. Show the source version and retrieval time near each passage. Render retrieved content as untrusted text or sanitized markup, and never treat instructions embedded in a source document as reviewer instructions. Avoid loading executable third-party content inside the review panel.

Avoid showing a preferred model name or a previous reviewer's verdict before an independent judgment. For pairwise comparisons, randomize answer order and include appropriate tie or neither-acceptable outcomes.

Design for keyboard use, visible focus, readable text, and explicit selection states. Keep evidence and the answer accessible without requiring excessive horizontal scrolling.

Start all judgment controls unselected and validate them on submission. Use labeled radio groups, an accessible error summary, and visible saving/submission status. A failed save should preserve the draft. Disable duplicate submissions in the UI, but enforce duplicate handling on the server as well.

Practical check: observe a reviewer completing several borderline examples. Record where they pause, misinterpret a label, or cannot find the necessary source material.

When two reviewers disagree, investigate before reducing their decisions to a majority vote.

Different assumptions about the user's expertise.

A genuine error by one or both reviewers.

Preserve independent labels and store the adjudicated result separately. This allows the team to study ambiguity instead of erasing it.

For two reviewers applying categorical labels to the same items, scikit-learn provides Cohen's kappa:

from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score

("q1", "a1", "s1", "auth-v1"): "supported",

("q2", "a1", "s2", "auth-v1"): "unsupported",

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "supported",

("q4", "a1", "s4", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported"

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported"

raise ValueError("Review sets must contain identical items")

raw_agreement = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(left, right)) / len(keys)

print(f"Raw agreement: {raw_agreement:.2f}")

print(f"Kappa: {cohen_kappa_score(left, right):.2f}")

This toy example prints raw agreement of 0.75 and kappa of about 0.64. Four items are not enough to assess a review program. In production, check for duplicate reviews before building dictionaries, use one rubric version per comparison, report unmatched items, and align all records by item, answer revision, and evidence snapshot.

Kappa measures agreement beyond chance under its assumptions, not correctness. Inspect raw agreement, label frequencies, and the disagreement table alongside it. A single-category batch can make kappa undefined; report that limitation rather than substituting a reassuring score. Treat cannot_assess explicitly and report its frequency instead of silently excluding difficult cases.

If both reviewers apply the same flawed rubric consistently, agreement can be high while the evaluation remains unhelpful.

Once difficult cases are adjudicated, turn them into regression cases with explicit acceptance criteria. For the fictional authentication task: use version 3 evidence, cite the passage requiring Bearer, and do not invent a header. If version 3 evidence is missing, an acceptable response should explain the gap rather than provide confident instructions.

Expected behavior or acceptance criteria.

DVC can track larger datasets alongside Git. In an existing Git repository with DVC initialized and data/reviewed-auth.jsonl present, a minimal versioning step is:

git add data/reviewed-auth.jsonl.dvc data/.gitignore

git commit -m "Version authentication review cases"

This commits metadata, not the dataset bytes. Configure an access-controlled DVC remote and push the data before expecting another machine or CI runner to retrieve it. Keep credentials and sensitive review material out of public repositories.

Keep development examples separate from held-out evaluation cases. If developers repeatedly tune prompts against the same questions, those questions become less useful as evidence of generalization.

Split related examples together where appropriate. Near-duplicate questions from one support conversation should not be scattered across development and evaluation sets.

Use two evaluation passes. First, hold the evidence snapshot fixed to compare answer-generation changes. Then test retrieval against the intended document versions to detect stale or irrelevant sources. Record per-item outcomes and report failures by category; an overall improvement can hide a regression in version-specific or multilingual questions.

SitePoint’s article on testing nondeterministic AI behavior provides further context for repeatable evaluation workflows.

A correct answer can still fail in the interface.

Users may overlook a caveat, misunderstand whether an operation has been performed, or miss that the evidence applies to an older API version.

Pair answer review with practical usability tasks:

Find the authentication requirements for version 3 and identify the source that supports them.

Observe whether users complete the task and whether their confidence matches the available evidence.

SitePoint’s overview of user research methods helps distinguish task observation from preference surveys.

Turn interface failures into browser tests: a citation opens the expected document version, its passage ID matches the displayed evidence, missing evidence offers a recovery action, and a failed review submission preserves the draft. Verify that reviewers cannot access unassigned restricted items by changing an ID in the URL. These checks complement human judgments; they do not replace them.

Do not use a fluent response as a substitute for a clear interaction. The interface should distinguish retrieved information, generated interpretation, and actions the application has actually completed.

Start with one authentication task, a versioned rubric, and a small calibration batch. Use Pydantic for ingestion checks, Label Studio or a custom interface for review, scikit-learn for agreement analysis, and Git/DVC for dataset provenance. Add each tool only when it solves a concrete workflow need.

At release time, run deterministic checks for schema, evidence references, permissions, and interface behavior. Compare candidate answers against adjudicated acceptance criteria and send new ambiguous failures back for review. Record the dataset revision and configurations with the results so another developer can reproduce the comparison.

The purpose of human review is to produce evidence the team can act on. A smaller collection of well-defined, traceable judgments is often more useful than a large pile of ratings whose meaning nobody can explain.

#10693. Trace & Evaluate your Agent with Arize Phoenix

So, you’ve built your agent. It takes in inputs and tools, processes them, and generates responses. Maybe it’s making decisions, retrieving information, executing tasks autonomously, or all three. But now comes the big question – how effectively is it performing? And more importantly, how do you know?

Building an agent is one thing; understanding its behavior is another. That’s where tracing and evaluations come in. Tracing allows you to see exactly what your agent is doing step by step—what inputs it receives, how it processes information, and how it arrives at its final output. Think of it like having an X-ray for your agent’s decision-making process. Meanwhile, evaluation helps you measure performance, ensuring your agent isn’t just functional, but actually effective. Is it producing the right answers? How relevant are its findings at each step? How well-crafted is the agent’s response? Does it align with your goals?

Arize Phoenix provides a centralized platform to trace, evaluate, and debug your agent's decisions in real time—all in one place. We’ll dive into how you can implement them to refine and optimize your agent. Because building is just the beginning—true intelligence comes from knowing exactly what’s happening under the hood.

For this, let’s make sure that we have an Agent setup! You can follow along with the following steps or use your own agent.

Once your agent is running, the next challenge is making sense of its internal workflow. Tracing helps you track each step your agent takes—from invoking tools to processing inputs and generating responses—allowing you to debug issues, optimize performance, and ensure it behaves as expected.

To enable tracing, we’ll use Arize Phoenix for visualization, and OpenTelemetry + OpenInference for instrumentation.

Once your agent is up and its run is monitored, the next step is to assess its performance. Evaluations (evals) help determine how well your agent is retrieving, processing, and presenting information.

There are many types of evals you can run, such as response relevance, factual accuracy, latency, and more. Check out the Phoenix documentation for a deeper dive into different evaluation techniques.

In this example, we’ll focus on evaluating the DuckDuckGo search tool used by our agent. We’ll measure the relevance of its search results using a Large Language Model (LLM) as a judge—specifically, OpenAI's GPT-4o.

#10692. A Deepdive into Aya Vision: Advancing the Frontier of Multilingual Multimodality

With the release of the Aya Vision family, our new 8B and 32B parameter vision-language models (VLMs), we are addressing one of the biggest challenges in AI: bringing multilingual performance to multimodal models.

Aya Vision is Cohere For AI's latest open-weight multilingual and multimodal model family, designed to be a strong foundation for language and vision understanding across 23 languages. It builds on the success of Aya Expanse, state-of-the-art multilingual language models, and extends it using a combination of advanced techniques. These include synthetic annotations, scaling up multilingual data through translation and rephrasing, and multimodal model merging – key methods that improve both language and vision understanding in a multilingual setting.

As a result, our models perform well in a variety of tasks, including image captioning, visual question answering, text generation, and translating both text and images into clear, natural-language text. We evaluated Aya Vision models on a set of datasets, including our new open-ended vision-language benchmark AyaVisionBench and a multilingual version of Wild Vision Bench (mWildVision) that is translated into 23 languages, which we release both of them for research.

In pair-wise comparison, Aya Vision 32B outperforms models more than 2x of its size, such as Llama-3.2 90B Vision, Molmo 72B, and Qwen2.5-VL 72B by win rates ranging from 50% to 64% on AyaVisionBench and 52% to 72% on mWildVision average across 23 languages.

Our compact and more efficient model Aya Vision 8B achieves the best performance in multilingual multimodal in its parameter class, outperforming leading models such as Qwen2.5-VL 7B, Pixtral 12B, Gemini Flash 1.5 8B, Llama-3.2 11B Vision, Molmo-D 7B, and Pangea 7B by up to 79% win-rates on AyaVisionBench and 81% on mWildBench.

We release both 8B and 32B models as open weights for the research community to further accelerate multilingual multimodal progress. In this blog post, we share the key technical details behind Aya Vision models

For a high-performance vision-language model, it is important to process images with arbitrary resolutions, especially high-resolution images. To enable this capability in Aya Vision, we dynamically resize and split any higher-resolution images into multiple tiles to generate rich image features from the image encoder. In Aya Vision models, we use the recently released SigLIP2-patch14-384 model as the initialization for the vision encoder.

While dynamic resizing enables processing high-resolution images, it also leads to a larger number of image tokens passing through the vision-language connector and LLM decoder. To improve latency and throughput, we use a downsampling method called Pixel Shuffle, to compress the number of image tokens by 4x. After downsampling, image tokens are aligned to the language model input embeddings through a vision-language connector and passed to an LLM decoder.

For the text decoder, we use our multilingual language models. For Aya Vision 8B, we use an LLM that is initialized from Cohere Command R7B for improved instruction following and world knowledge and further post-trained using the Aya Expanse recipe consisting of diverse multilingual data, model merging, and preference training. For Aya Vision 32B, we initialize the language model from Aya Expanse 32B based on its state-of-the-art multilingual performance.

We trained Aya Vision models in 2 stages – vision-language alignment and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In the vision-language alignment stage, only the vision-language connector is trained, while the vision encoder and the language model weights are kept frozen. This enables rudimentary vision-language understanding by mapping the image encoder features to the language model embedding space. In the SFT stage, we train both the connector and the language model on a diverse set of multimodal tasks in 23 languages.

One of the biggest challenges in developing a multilingual vision-language model is ensuring strong performance across underrepresented languages. To address this, we first gather synthetic annotations using a diverse pool of high-quality datasets in English, which lay the basis for our multilingual multimodal annotation. Following the synthetic annotations of English datasets, we translated a large volume of the data into 23 languages. To avoid translation artefacts and maintain fluent textual characteristics with high precision in answers, we then rephrased translated prompt/generation pairs by matching them with the original high-quality synthetic samples, expanding language coverage where real-world datasets are scarce. This improves both linguistic fluency and alignment between vision and text, allowing Aya Vision to exhibit superior image understanding in multiple languages.

Our 8B model, when only supervised fine-tuned with original academic datasets, reaches a 40.9% win rate across 23 languages in AyaVisionBench against Pangea 7B, which is a multilingual VLM, whereas synthetic annotations and scaling up the multilingual data lead to a 58.1% win rate with a gain of 17.2%. This significant improvement showcases the impact of significant investment in multilingual data coverage.

A state-of-the-art vision-language model should excel not only in image understanding but also in conversational context, where the model is expected to generate a high-quality response to both image and text inputs. To address this, inspired by our previous research on model merging, a technique that combines multiple trained models, we merge the base language model with the fine-tuned vision-language model.

Model merging enhances the generative capabilities of our final model that leads to a 70% win rates across 23 languages on AyaVisionBench against Pangea 7B, improving the multimodal win rate by 11.9% compared to the model before merging.

Multimodal model merging also enables our Aya Vision models to excel in text-only tasks as measured in mArenaHard datasets compared with the other leading vision-language models.

Finally, we scale our recipe from 8B to 32B, resulting in the state-of-the-art open-weight multilingual vision-language model – Aya Vision 32B which shows significant improvements in win rates due to the stronger initialization of the text-backbone, and outperforms models more than 2x of its size, such as Llama-3.2 90B Vision, Molmo 72B, and Qwen2.5-VL 72B by win rates ranging from 49% to 63% on AyaVisionBench and 52% to 72% on mWildVision average across 23 languages.

Together with Aya Vision models, we also release a high-quality multilingual vision-language benchmark called AyaVisionBench, constructed based on real-world applications, covering 23 languages and 9 distinct task categories, with 135 image-question pairs per language.

We make this evaluation set available to the research community to push forward multilingual multimodal evaluations. This dataset is designed to assess a model’s ability to perform a diverse range of vision-language tasks, including captioning, chart and figure understanding, identifying differences between two images, general visual question answering, OCR, document understanding, text transcription, reasoning involving logic and math, and converting screenshots to code. By incorporating multiple languages and task types, the dataset provides a broad and challenging evaluation framework for assessing cross-lingual and multimodal understanding.

To create this dataset, we first selected images from the Cauldron held-out test set, a large collection derived from 50 high-quality datasets, ensuring they had not been seen during training. For each image, we then generated a corresponding question that explicitly required visual context for an answer. These questions were synthetically generated and subsequently refined through a two-stage verification process. First, human annotators reviewed and validated each question to ensure it was clear, relevant, and truly dependent on the image. This rigorous selection and validation process ensures that the dataset serves as a robust benchmark for evaluating vision-language models in multilingual and real-world settings.

Communication happens in many forms and in many languages. With our leading research and development, we’ve released a model that facilitates connection, whether in text or visual, in 23 different languages today.

Aya Vision has a wide range of practical applications, where one notable example is its availability on WhatsApp, one of the most broadly used communications platforms in the world. This allows a massive audience of global citizens who speak a multitude of languages to utilize the capabilities of Aya Vision on a platform they use to communicate every single day.

Download weights and datasets from the Aya Vision collection on Hugging Face.Try Aya Vision using our Hugging Face Space or text it on WhatsappBuild on Aya using our colab example.

Learn more about our ongoing efforts around multilingual.

It also wouldn’t have been possible without the wider Cohere For AI and Cohere team who supported in many different ways. Special thanks to Sungjin Hong, Michael Kozakov, Pierre Richemond, Brittawnya Prince, Jim Payne, Kyle Lastovica, Jeff Colen, Jenna Cook, Viraat Aryabumi, Trent Fowler, Linus Chui, Meor Amer, Lucas Fayoux, Kyle Lastovica, Billy Trend, Acyr Locatelli, Morgan Norman, Florian Strub, Jon Ander Campos, Nick Frosst, Phil Blunsom, Aidan Gomez, Ivan Zhang.
